howDoI.q: How do I check that my colors work for players who see colors differently?
How do I make danger and safety look different by more than color?
How do I mark a safe path so it stands out?

pages.head: Welcome
pages.html:
Welcome

Colors That Work is a Starter: a small game that shows a few Game-Maker ideas, with signs in the levels that say what you are looking at. It has two short levels about colors that everyone can tell apart, and takes a few minutes to finish.

Some players see colors differently, and red and green can look alike to them. Play it first. Then open it in Game-Maker (Edit a copy on the home page keeps the original safe) and read the pages below, which say where each idea is made.

The keys

Left and Right walk. Space jumps. F2 shows your hit points, lives and score. Walk into the door at the end of a level to go on.

pages.head: Level 1: Red and Green
pages.html:
Level 1: Red and Green

The level card comes first, then two more pictures of the same row of plates: one as you see it, and one as a player who sees red and green alike can see it. In the second, every plate looks the same.

In the level, six flat plates lie in a row. The RED PLATES STING. GREEN ONES ARE SAFE sign says which is which, and the SOME PLAYERS SEE RED AND GREEN ALIKE sign says why that is a problem. Walk across: each red plate takes 5 hit points, once, and Yana shows her hurt pose. The plates are the same size and shape, with the same three rivets, so color is the only thing that tells them apart. Three coins are worth ten points each.

pages.head: How this level is made
pages.html:
How level 1 is made

  • Two plates, one shape. Open colors.bbl in the blocks editor. plateHot and plateSafe are drawn the same, pixel for pixel, in different colors. Only plateHot has Hit points set to −5, and Becomes block set to spent, a flat gray plate, so it stings once.
  • Colors that look alike to some players. Open colors.pal in the palette editor. The red and the green are picked so that a player who sees red and green alike sees nearly the same color for each. Which pairs do that is something you can work out with a color-vision simulator; the editor does not show it.
  • The second picture. The level card is a slide list, one.lst. It shows one.gif, then oneview.gif, then onealike.gif. The last two are the same picture saved with a different palette: the same numbers, drawn in other colors.
  • Where they are. Open one.map in the map editor. The plates are six blocks along the grass, painted like anything else.
  • The exit. A scene link joins the door to the next level. Open colors.gam in the scenes editor.

pages.head: Level 2: Shape and Brightness
pages.html:
Level 2: Shape and Brightness

The same stretch of ground, made to read in any color. The SPIKES LOOK LIKE SPIKES, IN ANY COLOR sign comes first: the things that sting are pointed spikes, dark at the foot. The LIGHT AND STRIPED MEANS SAFE sign says what the safe plates are: light, with upright stripes, like a crossing. The spikes are still red, and that is fine, because nothing depends on it now. The level card's second picture shows the same row as a player who sees red and green alike: the spikes still look like spikes and the plates still look like plates.

Jump the spikes and walk the plates, and nothing stings. Three coins are on the way.

pages.head: How this level is made
pages.html:
How level 2 is made

  • Shape. In colors.bbl, spikeRed is pictured as two pointed spikes. A pointed outline is read at a glance, and it does not change with color. spikeRed has Hit points −5 and becomes spent, like the red plate before.
  • Brightness and pattern. plateStripe is nearly white with teal stripes: lighter than the spikes by a wide margin, so even a gray picture keeps them apart. It has no hit points.
  • Checking. Look at your level with the color taken out, or through a simulator. If you can still say which is danger and which is safe, so can everyone. This game was checked that way, with the color-vision matrices of Machado, Oliveira and Fernandes (2009).
  • Where they are. Open two.map. The plates and spikes are blocks on the grass.

pages.head: What it cannot do
pages.html:
What it cannot do

Game-Maker has no color checker, and these are the limits:

  • It cannot check colors for you. It will not tell you that two colors look alike to some players. You have to look, or use a color-vision simulator outside Game-Maker, as this game's tools did.
  • It cannot switch palettes for a player. A player cannot choose a color-blind palette while playing; the scene's palette is the palette. If you want that, you would make a second scene with a second palette, and link to it yourself.
  • A scene has 256 colors at most, and color 0 is the background. Color 255 is see-through in a picture. A color you pick has to come out of that one list. Each color's red, green and blue go from 0 to 63, so two colors you meant to be different can land close together.
  • A picture's brightness is only what you draw. Game-Maker will not warn you that a light plate sits on a light floor.
  • The second pictures on the level cards are ordinary pictures made with another palette. Nothing in the engine simulates anything.

pages.head: Make it yours
pages.html:
Make it yours

Try one change at a time, and play after each:

  • In colors.bbl, change plateStripe's stripes to another color, and see if it is still easy to tell from a spike.
  • Make plateSafe a very different green, and see how the level card's second picture changes.
  • Make spikeRed green. It stings all the same, and it still looks like a spike.
  • Give a safe plate the red color, to see how much the stripes carry on their own.
  • Make plateHot take 15 hit points, and count how many Yana can cross.

The home page's Starters tab has more small games like this one.
